content:
Ezekiel 23 is quoted in debates between Muslims and Christians more often than almost any other chapter of the prophets. Muslim speakers read out its most explicit verses and ask whether God speaks this way; Christian apologists reply that the chapter is an allegory, and that its critics have torn a few lines from it.[1]

Both sides have part of the truth. The chapter is an allegory with a serious prophetic message, and its wording is as explicit as its critics say.

This article aims to provide context to the chapter, insha'Allah, in five facts: what it means, what it condemns, how it is worded, and what its own scholars say of it. We honour every prophet God sent, as the Quran commands: "We make no distinction between one and another among them" (3:84).[2]

Ezekiel tells of two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, and then explains them: "As for their names, Samaria is Oholah, and Jerusalem Oholibah" (Ezekiel 23:4).[3]

Samaria was the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, taken by Assyria in 722 BCE. Jerusalem was the capital of Judah, taken by Babylon in 587 BCE. The two women are the two kingdoms, and their story is the story of their fall.

Oholah "doted on her lovers, on the Assyrians her neighbors" (23:5). Oholibah saw images of Babylonian officers painted on a wall, "all of them looking like princes", and "sent messengers to them into Chaldea" (23:14 to 16). She turns to Egypt as well.[3]

C. L. Crouch, writing on Ezekiel and the foreign nations, explains why a prophet would speak of treaties as adultery: in Ezekiel's world, diplomacy, loyalty to a treaty and religious allegiance overlapped.[4] To trust in an empire was to put a partner beside God.

Ezekiel states the charge without allegory as well. "You have played the prostitute after the nations, and because you are polluted with their idols" (23:30). "They have committed adultery with their idols. They have also caused their sons, whom they bore to me, to pass through the fire to them to be devoured" (23:37).[3]

That is the heart of the chapter: the worship of other gods, and children burned as offerings to them. A Muslim reader recognises the message. It is the call of every prophet to worship God alone, and we honour Ezekiel for delivering it.

The chapter's language goes far beyond what the allegory needs. Verses 3, 8 and 21 describe the sisters' bodies being handled, and verse 20 compares the Egyptian lovers to donkeys and horses in plainly sexual terms.[3] We cite those verses and leave them unquoted.

Bryan Bibb, a Christian scholar of the Hebrew Bible, has studied how English translations treat these chapters. He finds that translators often soften the sexual detail while keeping the violence done to the women in the story.[5] Readers of many Bibles therefore meet a milder chapter than the Hebrew.

Fokkelien van Dijk-Hemmes examined in Vetus Testamentum how Ezekiel 23 makes a woman into the metaphor for a nation's sin, and what that metaphor does to the way women are spoken of.[6] Bibb describes the punishments the chapter promises, stripping, mutilation and stoning at the hands of the lovers, as sexualised violence, and asks readers to resist it.[5]

Bruno Biermann, writing in lectio difficilior, reads the chapter's language of male power and the feminised city as one rhetoric that cannot be separated from its message.[7] These are Christian and Jewish scholars of the Bible, writing in its own journals.

The bottom line

Ezekiel 23 is an allegory of two kingdoms that trusted in empires and worshipped their gods, and its charge of idolatry and child sacrifice is the message of every prophet. We honour that message. Its wording is another matter: the explicit verses are real, translations soften them, and the chapter's own scholars find the imagery troubling.

The Quran speaks of the same sins with restraint. It tells the story of Joseph and the wife of his master without a word of the body, and it commands: "Nor come nigh to adultery: for it is a shameful (deed) and an evil" (17:32).[2] Al-Fārūqī taught that Islam faults the earlier scriptures in "their historical form, in the texts they accepted as scripture", and honours the revelation behind them.[8] Ezekiel 23 shows that difference plainly. We set out the wider question in our article on whether Islam teaches that the Bible was corrupted. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. The exchange is common in public debate. The Bismikaa archive answered it in Kelucahan di dalam Yehezkiel 23.
  2. Quran 3:84; 12:23 to 24; 17:32, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Ezekiel 23:1 to 49 (World English Bible).
  4. C. L. Crouch, "Ezekiel and the Foreign Nations", in The Oxford Handbook of Ezekiel (Oxford University Press, 2020), pp. 278–294.
  5. Bryan Bibb, "There's No Sex in Your Violence: Patriarchal Translation in Ezekiel 16 and 23", Review and Expositor 111, no. 4 (2014), pp. 337–345.
  6. Fokkelien van Dijk-Hemmes, "The Metaphorization of Woman in Prophetic Speech: An Analysis of Ezekiel XXIII", Vetus Testamentum 43, no. 2 (1993), pp. 162–170.
  7. Bruno Biermann, "Männliche Herrschaft und Körperdiskurse zwischen Feminisierung und Virilität in Ezechiel 23", lectio difficilior 2 (2021).
  8. Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd ed. (Herndon, VA: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992), chapter 2.
